messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Electrician
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 78

The incident occurs six months ago, in the damp laneway behind the hardware store. Leo is walking home from a late shift, his tool belt heavy against his hips, when a man steps from behind a rusted fence gate. There is no warning—just a sharp crack to the back of his head, the cold press of a blade against his ribs, the forced shuffle of feet as they take his wallet and phone. The attacker’s breath smells of stale tobacco and salt air. Leo lies on the wet concrete, listening to footsteps fade, his hands trembling around a dropped torque wrench. He tells himself he will be fine, that it was just a robbery, that the body heals faster than the mind. In the weeks that follow, the shortcuts through the laneways disappear. He begins checking the workshop locks three times, then a fourth. The smell of damp concrete in his own garage sends his chest tight. He starts sleeping on the couch, his back pressed to the wall, a heavy wrench within reach despite his partner’s quiet pleas. When he finally lies in bed, his mind snaps back to the cold floor, the weight of the boot on his chest, the way the attacker’s eyes don’t blink. He wakes gasping, sweat soaking through his shirt, his heart hammering against his ribs like a live wire. He tells himself it’s just shock. He tells himself it will pass. At work, the changes creep in quietly. Leo used to love the rhythm of his trade—the clean snap of circuit breakers, the hum of a properly wired panel, the quiet satisfaction of seeing lights come on. Now, the clang of a ladder rung against a metal stud sounds like a footstep. When a new apprentice walks up behind him to hand him a roll of wire, Leo flinches so hard he drops his pliers. He starts avoiding solo jobs, requesting he always be paired with someone he knows. He tells himself it’s for safety, for efficiency. But the truth sits heavier: he can’t stand the silence of empty rooms, the way shadows pool in corners where a person could hide. He checks every junction box twice, then a third time, his fingers tracing the insulation like he’s searching for a fault line. His partner, Maya, notices the distance. She finds him staring at the television static, his jaw clenched so tight it aches. He pulls away when she tries to hug him, his shoulders tensing before his brain catches up. He doesn’t know how to explain that touch sometimes feels like a trap, that the gentle weight of a hand on his shoulder makes his pulse jump. They talk about it sometimes, but the words always feel stuck in his throat. He thinks about his grandfather’s stories, about men who never spoke of what broke them, who just worked until their hands forgot. He tries to carry the weight the same way—steadily, silently, without complaint. But the quiet is becoming a different kind of noise. Now, at forty-two, Leo walks through his days with a constant, low hum of alertness. He stands near exits at cafés. He maps escape routes before he sits down. He avoids news stories about street violence, changing the radio channel the moment a siren wails in the background. Sometimes, late at night, he sits on the back steps with a glass of water, watching the moonlight spill over the fence, trying to remember what it felt like to simply be still. He knows he survived it. He knows the blade never found its mark. But his nervous system keeps waiting for the next swing, and the world feels perpetually one step away from safe.
